::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Confine a wave between two boundaries and only certain frequencies survive. Those are the harmonics, and they are why instruments have pitch.
:::

## Two waves travelling in opposite directions

When two identical waves travel in **opposite directions** (such as when a wave on a guitar string reflects back and forth between two clamped bridge endpoints), they combine into a **standing wave**:

$$y(x, t) = A \sin(kx - \omega t) + A \sin(kx + \omega t) = \underbrace{2A \sin(kx)}_{\text{Spatial Profile}} \cdot \underbrace{\cos(\omega t)}_{\text{Temporal Oscillation}}$$

Notice that the wave **no longer travels**! Instead:

- **Nodes ($N$)**: Points where $\sin(kx) = 0 \implies y = 0$ at all times. Zero motion.
- **Antinodes ($A$)**: Points where $\sin(kx) = \pm 1 \implies$ Maximum oscillation amplitude $2A$.

```{=html}
</svg>
<figcaption><strong>Figure 1 | A clamped string is a frequency filter: it admits only the wavelengths that place a node at each end.</strong> Two identical waves travelling in opposite directions superpose into $y = 2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)$, a pattern that no longer moves — the shape stays put while the whole string breathes in and out of it. Nodes (magenta) sit where $\sin(kx) = 0$ and never move at all; antinodes swing through $2A$. Because both clamps must be nodes, the string length is forced to be a whole number of half-wavelengths, $L = n\lambda_n/2$, which quantises the allowed frequencies to $f_n = n\,v/2L$. That integer series is the harmonic series, and it is the reason a plucked string sounds like a pitch rather than a noise.</figcaption>
</figure>
```


The boundary condition that both ends of a string of length $L$ must be stationary nodes ($y(0)=0$ and $y(L)=0$) restricts standing waves to discrete **quantized frequencies**:

$$L = n \frac{\lambda_n}{2} \implies f_n = n \cdot \frac{v}{2L} = n \cdot f_1 \quad (n = 1, 2, 3, \dots)$$

This discrete set of natural resonant frequencies is the **Harmonic Series** that creates musical pitch, scales, and timbre!

### Where the product form comes from

The step from a sum of two travelling waves to a product of a spatial factor and a temporal factor is the identity $\sin a + \sin b = 2\sin\frac{a+b}{2}\cos\frac{a-b}{2}$. With $a = kx - \omega t$ and $b = kx + \omega t$, the half-sum is $kx$ and the half-difference is $-\omega t$, and since cosine is even the result is $2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)$. Every point on the string oscillates in step at the same frequency $\omega$; what differs from point to point is only the amplitude, $2A\sin(kx)$. Nothing moves along the string, which is why the pattern is called standing.

The nodes are spaced half a wavelength apart, since $\sin(kx)$ vanishes every time $kx$ advances by $\pi$, and the antinodes sit midway between them. That spacing is what the clamps select on: a string of length $L$ can only hold a whole number of half-wavelengths.

### Other boundary conditions

A string is fixed at both ends, but a column of air is not, and the boundary condition changes which harmonics survive.

| System | Ends | Condition | Allowed frequencies |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| String (guitar, piano, violin) | Both fixed | Displacement node at each end | $f_n = n\,v/2L$, all $n$ |
| Pipe open at both ends (flute, open organ pipe) | Both open | Displacement antinode at each end | $f_n = n\,v/2L$, all $n$ |
| Pipe closed at one end (clarinet, stopped organ pipe) | One closed, one open | Node at the closed end, antinode at the open end | $f_n = n\,v/4L$, odd $n$ only |

A pipe closed at one end has to fit a quarter-wavelength rather than a half, so its fundamental is an octave below an open pipe of the same length, and it sounds only the odd harmonics $f_1, 3f_1, 5f_1, \dots$. That missing set of even harmonics is the hollow spectrum of the clarinet that appears in the Fourier module, and it comes straight from the geometry of the bore.

### A worked example

A guitar's A string has scale length $L = 0.65\text{ m}$ and is tuned to $f_1 = 110\text{ Hz}$. From $f_1 = v/2L$, the wave speed on the string is

$$v = 2 L f_1 = 2 \times 0.65 \times 110 = 143\text{ m/s}$$

Fretting at the twelfth fret halves the vibrating length to $0.325\text{ m}$, and since $v$ has not changed, $f_1$ doubles to $220\text{ Hz}$: the octave, exactly as on Pythagoras' monochord. Tuning works on the other variable. Because $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$,

$$f_1 = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$$

so raising the pitch by a semitone (a factor of $2^{1/12} \approx 1.059$) requires raising the tension by a factor of $1.059^2 \approx 1.12$, about $12\%$. Doubling the pitch would need four times the tension, which is why the octave is played by shortening the string rather than tightening it, and why bass strings are made heavier (larger $\mu$) rather than longer or slacker.

### Resonance

A standing wave is what a bounded medium does when left to itself; **resonance** is what it does when pushed. Drive the string at an arbitrary frequency and the reflected waves return out of step with the driving, adding sometimes and cancelling sometimes, so the response stays small. Drive it at one of the $f_n$ and every reflection arrives in phase with the drive: energy is added on every cycle and the amplitude grows until losses balance the input. A child on a swing is pushed once per period for the same reason, and a singer who holds a glass's natural frequency can feed it energy faster than it dissipates.

Plucking a string is a broadband push: it excites many harmonics at once, in proportions that depend on where the string is struck. Plucking at the exact midpoint cannot excite the even harmonics, because each of them has a node there, so the tone is rounder; plucking near the bridge excites many high harmonics and the tone is bright. The set of harmonics an instrument sounds, and their relative strengths, is its timbre, and the interactive bench below shows the two ingredients, travelling waves and their superposition, that produce it.

## Interactive wave mechanics laboratory

Explore wave motion, longitudinal compression, and standing wave interference interactively below.

```{=html}
<div style="background: var(--md-code-bg-color, #1e293b); border: 1px solid #334155; border-radius: 12px; padding: 20px; margin: 24px 0; color: #f8fafc; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;">
  <div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 10px; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; margin-bottom: 16px;">
    <div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 8px;">
      <button id="btn-mode-travel" onclick="setWaveMode('traveling')" style="background: #2563eb; color: white; border: none; padding: 7px 14px; border-radius: 6px; cursor: pointer; font-weight: 600;">〰️ Traveling Wave</button>
      <button id="btn-mode-standing" onclick="setWaveMode('standing')" style="background: #334155; color: white; border: none; padding: 7px 14px; border-radius: 6px; cursor: pointer; font-weight: 600;">🔁 Standing Wave (Interference)</button>
      <button id="btn-mode-long" onclick="setWaveMode('longitudinal')" style="background: #334155; color: white; border: none; padding: 7px 14px; border-radius: 6px; cursor: pointer; font-weight: 600;">🔊 Longitudinal (Sound Particles)</button>
    </div>
    <div style="font-size: 0.85em; color: #94a3b8;">
      Mode: <strong id="mode-caption" style="color: #38bdf8;">Continuous Traveling Wave</strong>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(180px, 1fr)); gap: 14px; margin-bottom: 16px; background: rgba(0,0,0,0.25); padding: 12px; border-radius: 8px; font-size: 0.85em;">
    <div>
      <label>Frequency ($f$): <strong id="disp-freq" style="color: #38bdf8;">1.00</strong> Hz</label>
      <input type="range" id="slider-freq" min="0.2" max="3.0" step="0.1" value="1.0" oninput="updateWaveParams()" style="width: 100%; accent-color: #38bdf8;">
    </div>
    <div>
      <label>Wavelength ($\lambda$): <strong id="disp-lambda" style="color: #10b981;">240</strong> px</label>
      <input type="range" id="slider-lambda" min="100" max="450" step="10" value="240" oninput="updateWaveParams()" style="width: 100%; accent-color: #10b981;">
    </div>
    <div>
      <label>Amplitude ($A$): <strong id="disp-amp" style="color: #f59e0b;">45</strong> px</label>
      <input type="range" id="slider-amp" min="10" max="75" step="5" value="45" oninput="updateWaveParams()" style="width: 100%; accent-color: #f59e0b;">
    </div>
  </div>

  <canvas id="wave-canvas" width="760" height="260" style="width: 100%; height: auto; background: #020617; border-radius: 8px; border: 1px solid #1e293b; display: block;"></canvas>

  <div id="wave-legend" style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; font-size: 0.8em; color: #64748b; margin-top: 8px;">
    <span>Blue line: Net Wavefront displacement y(x, t)</span>
    <span>Wave Speed v = λ · f = <strong id="disp-speed" style="color: #38bdf8;">240</strong> px/s</span>

```


Superposition plus boundary conditions gives the discrete harmonics $f_1, 2f_1, 3f_1, \dots$; the modules on the mathematics of music and the Fourier transform build directly on that result.

---

```{=html}
<script>
// --- INTERACTIVE WAVE SIMULATOR ---
let waveMode = 'traveling';
let waveAnimId = null;
let waveTime = 0;

let waveFreq = 1.0;
let waveLambda = 240;
let waveAmp = 45;

function setWaveMode(mode) {
  waveMode = mode;
  const btnTravel = document.getElementById('btn-mode-travel');
  const btnStanding = document.getElementById('btn-mode-standing');
  const btnLong = document.getElementById('btn-mode-long');
  const cap = document.getElementById('mode-caption');

  btnTravel.style.background = '#334155';
  btnStanding.style.background = '#334155';
  btnLong.style.background = '#334155';

  if (mode === 'traveling') {
    btnTravel.style.background = '#2563eb';
    cap.innerText = 'Continuous Traveling Transverse Wave';
  } else if (mode === 'standing') {
    btnStanding.style.background = '#10b981';
    cap.innerText = 'Standing Wave: Two Counter-Propagating Waves Interfering';
  } else if (mode === 'longitudinal') {
    btnLong.style.background = '#f59e0b';
    cap.innerText = 'Longitudinal Compression / Sound Particle Oscillations';
  }
}

function updateWaveParams() {
  waveFreq = parseFloat(document.getElementById('slider-freq').value);
  waveLambda = parseFloat(document.getElementById('slider-lambda').value);
  waveAmp = parseFloat(document.getElementById('slider-amp').value);

  document.getElementById('disp-freq').innerText = waveFreq.toFixed(2);
  document.getElementById('disp-lambda').innerText = Math.round(waveLambda);
  document.getElementById('disp-amp').innerText = Math.round(waveAmp);

  const speed = waveLambda * waveFreq;
  document.getElementById('disp-speed').innerText = Math.round(speed);
}

function drawWaveSandbox() {
  const canvas = document.getElementById('wave-canvas');
  if (!canvas) return;
  const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);

  waveTime += 0.016;
  const midY = canvas.height / 2;
  const k = (2 * Math.PI) / waveLambda;
  const omega = 2 * Math.PI * waveFreq;

  // Background equilibrium reference line
  ctx.strokeStyle = '#1e293b';
  ctx.lineWidth = 1;
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.moveTo(0, midY);
  ctx.lineTo(canvas.width, midY);
  ctx.stroke();

  if (waveMode === 'traveling') {
    // 1. Traveling Transverse Wave
    ctx.strokeStyle = '#38bdf8';
    ctx.lineWidth = 3;
    ctx.beginPath();
    for (let x = 0; x < canvas.width; x += 2) {
      const y = midY - waveAmp * Math.sin(k * x - omega * waveTime);
      if (x === 0) ctx.moveTo(x, y); else ctx.lineTo(x, y);
    }
    ctx.stroke();

    // Draw traveling crest marker beads
    for (let x = 30; x < canvas.width; x += 120) {
      const y = midY - waveAmp * Math.sin(k * x - omega * waveTime);
      ctx.fillStyle = '#f87171';
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(x, y, 4.5, 0, Math.PI * 2); ctx.fill();
    }

  } else if (waveMode === 'standing') {
    // 2. Standing Wave: y = 2A sin(kx) cos(wt)
    // Draw individual component traveling waves (faint)
    ctx.strokeStyle = 'rgba(56, 189, 248, 0.25)';
    ctx.lineWidth = 1.5;
    ctx.setLineDash([3, 4]);
    ctx.beginPath();
    for (let x = 0; x < canvas.width; x += 3) {
      const y1 = midY - (waveAmp * 0.7) * Math.sin(k * x - omega * waveTime);
      if (x === 0) ctx.moveTo(x, y1); else ctx.lineTo(x, y1);
    }
    ctx.stroke();

    ctx.strokeStyle = 'rgba(244, 63, 94, 0.25)';
    ctx.beginPath();
    for (let x = 0; x < canvas.width; x += 3) {
      const y2 = midY - (waveAmp * 0.7) * Math.sin(k * x + omega * waveTime);
      if (x === 0) ctx.moveTo(x, y2); else ctx.lineTo(x, y2);
    }
    ctx.stroke();
    ctx.setLineDash([]);

    // Net Standing Wave
    ctx.strokeStyle = '#10b981';
    ctx.lineWidth = 3.5;
    ctx.beginPath();
    for (let x = 0; x < canvas.width; x += 2) {
      const y = midY - (1.4 * waveAmp) * Math.sin(k * x) * Math.cos(omega * waveTime);
      if (x === 0) ctx.moveTo(x, y); else ctx.lineTo(x, y);
    }
    ctx.stroke();

    // Mark Nodes (Zero displacement points)
    const halfLambda = waveLambda / 2;
    for (let nx = 0; nx <= canvas.width; nx += halfLambda) {
      ctx.fillStyle = '#ef4444';
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(nx, midY, 5, 0, Math.PI * 2); ctx.fill();
      ctx.fillStyle = '#fca5a5';
      ctx.font = '10px system-ui';
      ctx.fillText('Node', nx - 12, midY + 18);
    }

  } else if (waveMode === 'longitudinal') {
    // 3. Longitudinal Compression Sound Particles
    const numRows = 7;
    const numCols = 38;
    const spacingX = canvas.width / numCols;
    const spacingY = 24;

    for (let r = 0; r < numRows; r++) {
      const py = midY - ((numRows - 1) * spacingY) / 2 + r * spacingY;

      for (let c = 0; c < numCols; c++) {
        const equilibriumX = c * spacingX + spacingX / 2;
        // Longitudinal horizontal displacement: dx = A cos(kx - wt)
        const dx = (waveAmp * 0.7) * Math.cos(k * equilibriumX - omega * waveTime);
        const px = equilibriumX + dx;

        // Color particles by local compression density
        const densityVal = Math.sin(k * equilibriumX - omega * waveTime);
        const particleColor = densityVal > 0 ? '#38bdf8' : '#f59e0b';

        ctx.fillStyle = particleColor;
        ctx.beginPath();
        ctx.arc(px, py, 3.5, 0, Math.PI * 2);
        ctx.fill();
      }
    }

    ctx.fillStyle = '#94a3b8';
    ctx.font = '11px system-ui';
    ctx.fillText('Density High (Compression)', 40, 30);
    ctx.fillText('Density Low (Rarefaction)', 420, 30);
  }

  waveAnimId = requestAnimationFrame(drawWaveSandbox);
}

function initWaveApp() {
  updateWaveParams();
  if (waveAnimId) cancelAnimationFrame(waveAnimId);
  waveAnimId = requestAnimationFrame(drawWaveSandbox);
}

if (typeof document$ !== 'undefined') {
  document$.subscribe(() => {
    initWaveApp();
  });
}
window.addEventListener('load', () => {
  initWaveApp();
});
setTimeout(() => {
  initWaveApp();
}, 250);
</script>
```


## Key takeaways

- Two identical waves travelling in opposite directions add to $y = 2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)$: a fixed spatial profile that oscillates in place rather than travelling.
- Nodes are the points where $\sin(kx) = 0$ and the string never moves; antinodes are where it swings through the full $2A$.
- Clamping both ends forces a node at $x = 0$ and $x = L$, so only wavelengths with $L = n\lambda_n/2$ survive.
- The allowed frequencies are $f_n = n\,v/2L = n f_1$, the harmonic series, and this discrete ladder is what gives a string or air column a definite pitch.
- A pipe closed at one end fits a quarter-wavelength and sounds only odd harmonics; resonance is the growth in amplitude when a drive matches one of these natural frequencies.
